questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Overhang / projection?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Bolada” = overhang / projection. Origin: Spanish voladizo/volada “jutting out”, from volar “to fly”. Filipino spelling swaps v for b.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Soffit?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sepeto / Intrados” = soffit. Intradós is borrowed from Spanish intradós “underside of an arch or soffit”. Sepeto: origin not confirmed. Memory hook: the soffit seals the underside of the eave.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Fascia board?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Senepa” = fascia board. Origin: Spanish cenefa “border, trim, valance”. Senepa is cenefa, the trim at the edge of the roof. The same term is also used for: plank board, riser, skirt.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Gutter is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Alulod / Kanal” = gutter. Origin: kanal is Spanish canal “channel”, the same word as English “canal”. Alulod is the native Filipino word for a water channel. The same term is also used for: conductor, groove.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Lean-to roof?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sibe” = lean-to roof. Origin of sibe not confirmed. Memory hook: a lean-to is a one-sided roof like an extended eave, so it shares the word sibe. The same term is also used for: eaves.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Ridge roll?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Caballete / Kaballete” = ridge roll. Origin: Spanish caballete “roof ridge”, literally “little horse”. The ridge runs along the roof like a horse's back.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Parapet?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Kuya / Muralya” = parapet. Origin: muralya from Spanish muralla “wall, rampart”. Memory aid: Kuya (big brother) stands guard at the roof edge.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Canopy?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Media Agua” = canopy. Origin: Spanish media agua “half water”: a single-slope roof that sheds rain to one side only. The same term is also used for: awning.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Gable roof is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Dos Aguas” = gable roof. Origin: Spanish dos aguas “two waters”: a roof that sheds rain to two sides.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Roof is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Atip, Bubong” = roof. Origin: Tagalog atip “thatch roofing” and bubong “roof, ridge”, the traditional house roof.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Eaves is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sibe / Alero” = eaves. Alero is borrowed from Spanish alero “eaves”, from ala “wing”: the roof's wings. Sibe: origin not confirmed; it also names the lean-to roof, so think of both as the sloping part that juts out. The same term is also used for: Lean-to roof.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Conductor?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Alulod” = conductor. Native Tagalog alulod “water channel”. Memory aid: the conductor leads rainwater down, like a channel. The same term is also used for: gutter.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Down spout?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tubo de Banado” = down spout. Likely origin: Spanish tubo de bajada “downpipe”, reshaped in Filipino speech to tubo de banado. Tubo = pipe, bajada = going down.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Slope?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Bahada” = slope. Origin: likely Spanish bajada “descent, slope”. Filipino spelling turns j into h, as in bajada, bahada.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Plain G.I. sheet is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Hiero Liso” = plain G.I. sheet. Origin: Spanish hierro “iron” + liso “smooth, plain”, so smooth iron sheet.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Awning?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Media Agua” = awning. Origin: Spanish media agua “half water”: a single-slope roof that sheds rain to one side only. The same term is also used for: canopy.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Corrugated G.I. sheets?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Hiero Kanalado” = corrugated G.I. sheets. Origin: Spanish hierro “iron” + canalado “grooved, channelled”, so channelled iron sheet.
